points: The specification defines the area as individual and co-operative activities that take place in a challenging environment, usually outdoors.
In these activities, elements that cannot be fully controlled influence the selection and use of the skills and strategies needed to attain set goals.
In each activity, learners aim to develop the standard of their performance, to be creative as an individual and/or team member, and to be consistent in the quality of their performance.
The area places a particular emphasis on interpersonal skills and on reflection on learning.

notes.h: The five activities and the choice rule
points: Learners study three activities, each from a different area, and one of the three is chosen from this area.
From this area, learners choose one of five activities: orienteering, canoeing or kayaking, rock-climbing, sailing, or rowing or sculling.
Uncontrollable elements include weather, wind, water conditions, terrain, visibility and daylight.
Performers must read these conditions and adapt their plan to them.
Visibility and daylight limit how far ahead a performer can plan a route.
The challenge comes from real but controlled risk.
Performers and leaders identify hazards and choose skills, equipment and plans that keep the danger within what the group can handle.
Interpersonal skills in a group include communication, trust, teamwork, leadership and decision-making.
Co-operation with a partner is essential: a belayer and climber depend on each other, and the crew in a boat must work together.
Reflection means reviewing decisions and the route or plan choices made in a session.
Reflection takes place after each session, so that the choices made in the next session can be improved.

notes.h: Safety management common to all activities
points: Risk assessment of the site and conditions comes before the activity starts.
Qualified instruction and supervision are required.
Weather and tide forecasts are checked before going out.
Equipment such as helmets, buoyancy aids and harnesses is checked before use.
The plan and the expected return time are told to someone who is not taking part.
Emergency and communication plans are in place, and first aid is available.
Group sizes and instructor-to-participant ratios are set to suit the activity and the site.
Respect for the environment is good practice in all adventure activities.
In practice it means taking litter home, staying on paths and avoiding disturbance to wildlife.
Respect for the environment is one of the skills listed for orienteering.
The performance assessment is carried out in one of the student's three activities.
It requires the listed skills and techniques, applied in a conditioned practice, a competitive version or a personal performance.
Tactical knowledge is assessed: the tactics and strategies used in the activity.
Rules, regulations, codes of practice and safe practice are assessed before, during and after the activity.

notes.h: Adventure activities as a context for theory
points: Confidence and anxiety management: adventure activities involve real but managed risk, so performers must control anxiety and build confidence step by step.
Decision-making under uncertainty can be tested, because conditions cannot be fully predicted or controlled.
Fitness demands are muscular endurance, cardio-respiratory endurance and balance.
Safe practice and the regulations that apply to an activity can be tested.
Outdoor and adventure activities also count as a concept of physical activity in the written exam, where questions use them as context for confidence, safety regulations and attire.

keyTerms.definition: Individual and co-operative activities in a challenging environment, usually outdoors, in which uncontrollable elements influence the choice and use of skills and strategies.
Conditions such as weather, wind, water, terrain, visibility and daylight that a performer cannot fully control.
The real but controlled risk that gives an adventure activity its challenge.
The communication, trust, teamwork, leadership and decision-making needed to work with others in a group.
Reviewing decisions and route or plan choices after a session in order to improve the next one.
A systematic check of the site and conditions that identifies hazards before an activity starts.
A flotation garment worn in water activities that keeps the wearer afloat.
A practice of skills under set conditions, rather than in a full competitive version.
Knowing which strategy to use in a given situation and why.

factCards.term: Five activities in the adventure activities area
factCards.definition: Orienteering, canoeing or kayaking, rock-climbing, sailing, rowing or sculling.

factCards.term: Safety checks before an adventure activity: name four
factCards.definition: Risk assessment of the site and conditions; checking weather and tide forecasts; checking equipment before use; telling someone the plan and return time.

factCards.definition: An environment that cannot be fully controlled; managed risk; interpersonal skills; reflection on learning.
Listed skills and techniques; tactical knowledge; rules, regulations, codes of practice and safe practice.

questions.prompt: Describe two features of adventure activities and explain how each influences a performer's choice of skills and strategies.
questions.model: The first feature is uncontrollable elements. Weather, wind, water conditions, terrain, visibility and daylight cannot be fully controlled, so the performer must read them and choose skills and strategies that suit them. A sailor in strong gusts may choose a more cautious course, and an orienteer in poor visibility may choose a route that follows a handrail. The second feature is managed risk. The challenge comes from real but controlled risk, so the performer chooses skills and plans that keep the danger within what the group can handle, and these choices are made with partners, so interpersonal skills such as communication and trust shape the strategy used.

questions.prompt: Outline three safety measures that should be taken before an adventure activity.
questions.model: First, a risk assessment of the site and conditions identifies the hazards and the people who could be harmed, so that the plan can control them. Second, weather and tide forecasts are checked, so that the activity is not started in conditions beyond the group's ability. Third, equipment such as helmets, buoyancy aids and harnesses is checked before use, so that faults are found before the activity begins.
